mappings.note: Plain http is accepted only for loopback endpoints or with the oauth.allowInsecureHttp escape hatch of the server configuration. The rule covers the authorization server itself and its authorization and token endpoints at discovery, before anything is sent there, and the registration endpoint where a client registers: the OAuth client before its dynamic registration (with a configured prompt it asks for client credentials instead, as the product's providers do), and the product's dynamic authentication provider before it registers, at creation (by the creating server's escape hatch) or after invalid_client (by the escape hatch of the server whose request it serves: a provider is shared by the servers and the agent host that use the same authorization server and resource, and the workbench passes each server's rules with its requests); a pre-registered or Client ID Metadata Document client never contacts it, so a plain-HTTP registration endpoint does not fail discovery. The device authorization endpoint follows the same rule where the product's device code flow uses it, before its first request. The agent host's MCP sign-in creates its providers only from metadata whose issuer is the authorization server and whose authorization server, authorization, token and device authorization endpoints follow the rule (without an escape hatch). The enterprise-managed (XAA) sign-in applies the same rule, escape hatch included, to the resource authorization server it fetches metadata from and to the token endpoint that metadata names, before the IdP sign-in.

mappings.reason: Schemas are validated in their declared or default dialect, except one keyword: a pattern (or patternProperties key) that the backtracking guard rejects (back-references, lookbehind, groups nested more than 64 deep, and repetitions it cannot prove linear: a repeated group with alternatives or of unbounded length, including nested unbounded quantifiers, and a group of varying length repeated without bound or so often that it can split a match in more than 256 ways), or that is not a regular expression with or without the u flag, is not asserted, and the schema's other keywords still are. Every other pattern gets a bound on the steps of one test, a polynomial in the input length for a backtracking matcher without V8's optimizations, read in the mode the pattern compiled in (without the u flag \u{3} is u three times): each character, class or assertion it examines is a step, a loop of 32 or more iterations (also a fixed count such as .{99999}) scans the input, a give-back that the rest of the pattern can start matching runs it again, a lookahead scans at every arrival, and an unanchored search runs at every position. A pattern whose bound exceeds 10 million steps already for strings of 64 characters (e.g. ^a*a*a*a*$ or \d+\d+\d+$, the fourth power of the input length) is not asserted; one whose bound grows faster than linearly or by more than 256 steps per character (e.g. ^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$, an unanchored a+b, ^a*.{4000}!, or a 4000-character sequence tried at every position) is asserted only on strings whose bound stays within 10 million steps (2234, 2235, 3160 and 2497 characters); nothing is asserted about longer ones. The client logs a warning instead of refusing the whole schema, which would drop the tool (basic#046 asks for such bounds, and a time budget cannot interrupt a single regular expression match; patterns that need the non-unicode mode, such as \- or \#, compile and are asserted).

mappings.note: Every gateway route rate-limits tools/call per client with a token bucket (default 50 a second, bursts of 100; IMcpGatewayServiceOptions.rateLimits configures or turns it off), on HTTP for both revisions and on gRPC. The specification names no error, so a call over the limit gets -32603 with data { reason: 'rate_limited', retryAfterMs, method, scope } (HTTP status 200; gRPC RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, the error in mcp-error-bin) and never reaches the server. A client is a 2026-07-28 client's address and _meta client info, a 2025-11-25 session, or a gRPC client's address and client info, kept as a fixed-size hash; an idle client's bucket is forgotten after 10 minutes. Since a client names itself, a route-wide bucket of 4 times the rate holds all clients together, so changing the client info or opening new sessions gains nothing. scope says which bucket refused the call: 'client' (the message says that this client sends too many) or 'route' (the message, and the gateway log, say that the server is busy).
